newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada sees difficulties in U.S. plan for Pol Pot.
newsitem.headline: Canada sees difficulties in U.S. plan for Pol Pot.

text.p: Canada will have a difficult time complying with a U.S. request to help extradite Khmer Rouge guerrilla chief Pol Pot from Cambodia, Canadian government officials said on Monday.

"It looks like Canada's involvement would be difficult because the legal structure is not in place," Jennifer Ledwidge, a spokeswoman for the Department of Foreign Affairs, said. "We would like to see Pol Pot brought to justice."

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright asked Canadian Foreign Affairs Minister Lloyd Axworthy over the weekend to use Canadian legislation to ask for the extradition of Pol Pot from Cambodia. Once he is extradited, the United States wants Canada to send him to an international tribunal to be tried, Ledwidge said.

"The minister made no commitments but he indicated he would see what we might be able to do," Axworthy's spokeswoman Catherine Lappe said by telephone on Monday. "The Americans were suggesting that Canada has the capacity to apply its domestic legislation in such a way that it can reach beyond our borders to prosecute or indict war criminals."

Canada has a clause in its criminal code that allows for prosecution for war crimes or crimes against humanity committed outside the country. But it does not have legislation that would enable it to extradite Pol Pot to an international tribunal, Ledwidge said.

In any case, she added, there had so far been no move to set up an international tribunal to try him. "Without the legal structure in place, there's nothing we could do today, but we're looking at the options."
Canada has not yet given a formal response to the United States, she said. The United States is also awaiting confirmation that Pol Pot is in custody.

Although Cambodian government leaders announced that he was being held by his former Khmer Rouge allies, a senior U.S. official said Washington was waiting for "absolute assurance that they have him. We don't have final confirmation."
More than one million people were killed as enemies of Pol Pot's revolution or died of disease, starvation or overwork during the Khmer Rouge's brutal 1975-79 rule.

If Canada agrees to seek his extradition the United States is ready to coordinate sending a military team to Cambodia to remove Pol Pot from the country, U.S. officials said. One official termed it a "parallel operation in terms of logistical assistance for the Cambodians so that Pol Pot can be safely and quickly brought to a holding location."

But Canadian officials said the Americans may be jumping the gun. "This is all premature," Lappe said. "We haven't had a chance to look at the details ... it was a corridor chat that we're just following up on."
Officials said Foreign Affairs was in contact with U.S. officials and would likely have a response ready soon but not on Monday.
